nodes.label: Resulting Trusts
nodes.summary: Nature of resulting trusts, presumed resulting trust, presumption of advancement, rebutting presumptions, Quistclose trusts, and the rule in Hancock v Watson.

nodes.label: Nature and Methodologies
nodes.summary: Resulting trusts arise in two situations: (A) voluntary transfers or purchase in the name of another (presumed resulting trust), and (B) failure to exhaust the beneficial interest of an express trust (automatic resulting trust). The rationale is presumed intention of the transferor.

nodes.label: Presumption of Resulting Trust
nodes.summary: Where person A provides money for property put in B's name, equity presumes a resulting trust in favour of A unless the relationship gives rise to a presumption of advancement.

nodes.label: Presumption of Advancement
nodes.summary: In certain relationships (father to child, husband to wife), equity presumes a gift rather than a resulting trust. The presumption can be rebutted by evidence of actual intention. Not extended to cohabitants or siblings generally.

nodes.label: Rebutting the Presumptions
nodes.summary: Both presumptions (resulting trust and advancement) can be rebutted by evidence of the transferor's actual intention. The court looks at all circumstances including subsequent conduct and statements.

nodes.label: Quistclose Trusts (Failure of Specific Purpose)
nodes.summary: Where money is advanced for a specific purpose and the recipient is not free to use it as his own, a primary trust arises. If the purpose fails, a secondary resulting trust for the lender arises. The intention to restrict the use of money must be communicated and acquiesced to.

nodes.label: The Rule in Hancock v Watson
nodes.summary: If an absolute gift has a trust engrafted onto it and the engrafted trust fails (e.g. for perpetuity), the original absolute gift takes effect. There is no resulting trust back to the settlor.

nodes.label: Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale v Islington London Borough Council [1996] AC 669 (HL)
nodes.summary: Nature of resulting trust: a property right arising to give effect to the presumed intention of the provider, not a remedy for unjust enrichment. Followed in HK.

nodes.label: Cheung Yuk Ying Engarcia v Macgregor Isabella [2003] 2 HKLRD 177
nodes.summary: Resulting trust: elder cousin's actual intention to hide shares from ex-husband by gifting them to younger cousin defeated resulting trust claim.

nodes.label: Yau Kwong-Chiu v Yau Kwong-Ha [2007] 3 HKLRD 692
nodes.summary: Presumption of advancement: survivorship in joint account proven a gift from mother to daughter. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Twinsectra Ltd v Yardley [2002] UKHL 12
nodes.summary: Quistclose trust: Lord Millett affirmed the Quistclose trust is an orthodox resulting trust. HK adoption requires verification.

nodes.label: Prickly Bay Waterside Ltd v British American Insurance Co Ltd [2022] UKPC 8
nodes.summary: Quistclose: intention need not be mutual; it is enough if the payer imposes the restriction and the recipient acquiesces.

nodes.label: Hancock v Watson [1902] AC 14 (HL)
nodes.summary: Rule in Hancock v Watson: absolute gift with engrafted trust failing results in original gift taking effect, not resulting trust.

nodes.label: Verify HK Quistclose and Resulting Trust Cases
nodes.summary: Research HK CFA/CA decisions on Quistclose trusts, resulting trusts and advancement. Confirm HK adoption of Twinsectra and Prickly Bay.
